cues.en: So let's now talk about something that is a talk I hoped I would not have to give. I did not plan to give until last month when I saw other talks about memory model and automics and I said there's just gotta be information in one place about this, including the parts we hoped never to have to teach. So over breakfast at our table we were discussing which was more cruel to you.
cues.zh: 现在我们来聊一个我本希望永远不用讲的话题。直到上个月我都没打算讲，但我看到其他关于内存模型和原子操作的演讲后，我觉得必须得有一处能把所有相关信息讲透，包括那些我们本希望永远不用教的部分。所以早餐时我们还在讨论，对你们来说哪种更残忍：

cues.en: to inflict a deep universal references talk on you yesterday, right after lunch, or to inflict a deep atomics and memory model talk on you, not only first thing in the morning when you barely had the chance to have your first hit of coffee, but through the entire morning up to lunchtime. And we decided both were equally cruel, so here we go. This talk is not only about stood atomics,
cues.zh: 是昨天刚吃完午饭就给你们灌输一场硬核的通用引用讲座，还是在大清早、你们甚至还没来得及喝上第一口咖啡的时候，就让你们听一场硬核的原子操作与内存模型讲座，而且还要一直讲到吃午饭。我们觉得两者同样残忍，所以咱们开始吧。这场演讲不仅关乎 std::atomic，

cues.en: It's about the whole C++ memory model, but with a focus on std atomics because first I want to cover the rules that apply to all kinds of synchronization including mutexes and condition variables and atomics. But then we'll delve specifically into atomics all the way down into the gory details of the hardware on several popular platforms and architectures to see the reasons why things are the way they are, where the hardware is today, and how it's moving in flight today.
cues.zh: 它探讨的是整个 C++ 内存模型，但重点会放在 std::atomic 上。因为我首先想讲讲适用于所有同步机制的规则，包括互斥锁、条件变量和原子操作。接着我们会专门深入剖析原子操作，一路下潜到几种主流平台和架构的底层硬件细节，看看事情为什么会是现在这样、当前硬件的发展现状，以及它正在朝什么方向演进。

cues.en: So we're going to start with defining basic things like races, optimizations, the memory model, and how those three things really go together and are important. We're then going to talk about ordering. So as Scott started speaking to in one of his review slides, what about acquire and release? What do those mean? And even if you've encountered those before, we're going to be really crisp. These are very fundamental concepts. And it turns out there's more than one kind of acquire and release.
cues.zh: 所以我们要先从基本概念讲起，比如数据竞争、优化、内存模型，以及这三者是如何紧密相变且至关重要的。接着我们会讲内存顺序。正如 Scott 在他的一页回顾幻灯片里提到的，acquire 和 release 到底是什么？它们意味着什么？即使你以前接触过，我们也会把它讲得非常透彻。这些都是非常基础的概念。事实证明，acquire 和 release 还不止一种，

cues.en: with a very slight but important difference. We're then going to talk about how this applies to all kinds of synchronization, butexes, atomics, and fences, and how to use each one, including why you almost never want to use standalone fences. Then we're going to talk about things that this implies for compilers and hardware that you shouldn't ever need to know, but sometimes hardware and compiler have bugs, especially as they're implementing this stuff.
cues.zh: 它们之间有着非常微小但极其关键的区别。然后我们会讲这些概念如何应用于各种同步机制——互斥锁、原子操作和内存屏障，以及如何使用它们，包括为什么你几乎永远不该使用独立的内存屏障。接着我们会讲这对于编译器和硬件意味着什么，这些本来是你完全不需要了解的，但有时硬件和编译器会出现 bug，尤其是在实现这些机制时。

cues.en: Or your program might have a race condition which exposes these things. We're going to talk about code generation performance on a slew of popular platforms. And then, because this talk probably doesn't fit in half a day, if we have time, we'll talk about relaxed atomics. This is the part I hope to never, ever, ever to have to teach. But unfortunately, maybe we do. And if we get to it, a coda on what volatile means and what it's for. Just a couple of slides, which you have.
cues.zh: 或者你的程序中可能存在暴露这些问题的竞争条件。我们还会讨论在众多主流平台上的代码生成性能。之后，因为这场演讲半天可能讲不完，如果有时间，我们会讲讲 relaxed 原子操作。这正是我原本极度希望永远、永远、永远不用教的部分。但不幸的是，我们可能不得不讲。如果还有时间，最后会收尾讲讲 volatile 的含义和用途。就几页幻灯片，你们手里也有。

cues.en: The goal is to get up to here. This is the important, most important stuff that you should be using. This is basically stuff that hopefully you shouldn't, but maybe you shouldn't, if so, why? And then the code. So let's start with that first section on optimizations, races, and memory model. This is the hardware that we all code for, that we would all love to code for. It's
cues.zh: 目标是讲到这。这是重要的、你最该用的东西。这些基本上是你希望自己不该用的东西，但也许你确实不该用；如果是，为什么？然后是代码。那我们从第一节开始：优化、竞态和内存模型。这就是我们写代码所面向、也乐于面向的硬件。它就是

cues.en: The classic von Neumann machine of a processor attached to storage. It's very easy to just find the order in which things happen. I've got a thread, it does this, it does this, it writes something to RAM, look, there it goes. It loads something back, look, it fetches it from RAM and it operates on RAM directly. Even in a multi-core world where we're no longer in a von Neumann architecture and never will be again, we still program with the same idea that although there may be more CPU cores,
cues.zh: 经典的冯·诺依曼机：处理器连接存储器。很容易确定事情发生的顺序。我有一个线程，它做这个，做那个，往 RAM 写点东西，看，就这么写了。它再加载回来，看，从 RAM 取回，并直接在 RAM 上操作。即使在多核世界里，我们已不再处于冯·诺依曼架构，也永远不会再回到那种架构，我们编程时仍然沿用同样的想法：虽然可能有更多 CPU 核心，

cues.en: We program with the idea that conceptually they operate one at a time. Each one has direct access to the memory and reads and writes directly from global memory at a time. That's our mental model. So that even if each of these cores is running a different thread, the operations interleave so that the end effect of your program is as if some interleaving of the operations of all your threads.
cues.zh: 我们编程时仍认为它们概念上一次只运行一个。每个核心都直接访问内存，并一次直接读写全局内存。这就是我们的心智模型。因此，即使每个核心运行不同线程，操作也会交错，使你程序的最终效果，就像所有线程的操作按某种顺序交错执行一样。

cues.en: Now, even the interleaving part sometimes makes people a little nervous, but it's not too bad because we protect things with critical regions, mutex lock, unlock, to make sure certain bad interleavings can't happen. And then we say, okay, those blocks somehow will interleave. And they may interleave differently from run to run. This is still the model we want to program for, but to get there, we have to make sure that we understand the memory model and obey the rules. Here is an actual piece of hardware, because here's the picture we'd like.
cues.zh: 现在，光是交错这部分有时就让人有点紧张，但没那么糟，因为我们用临界区、互斥锁加锁/解锁来保护，确保某些糟糕的交错不会发生。然后我们说，好吧，那些块反正会交错。而且每次运行的交错方式可能不同。这仍是我们想面向的模型，但要做到这一点，必须确保理解内存模型并遵守规则。这是一块真实的硬件，因为这才是我们想要的图景。

cues.en: Here's just a sample piece of hardware from four years ago that what we actually program. And you see peaks and valleys. You don't directly talk to RAM, which no longer fits on this slide to scale. It's somewhere, you know, covering the whole next 10 floors. You have 16 megavel 3 cache. On top of that, every pair of cores on the Intel Dunnington chip shares a 3 megabyte.
cues.zh: 这是四年前的一块示例硬件，也是我们实际编程的对象。你会看到波峰和波谷。你并不直接和 RAM 对话，它已经大到这张幻灯片按比例放不下了。它大概在某个地方，覆盖接下来十层楼。你有 16MB 三级缓存。在此基础上，Intel Dunnington 芯片上每一对核心共享 3MB 的

cues.en: in this particular configuration, L2 cache. On top of that, each core individually has its own L1 cache. Oh, and importantly, a store buffer, because writes are always more expensive than reads, and so you really want to cache those and buffer those. And this is, if you squint at it just right, you'll see a mountain range of memory, peaks, each with a core sitting on top. This is very far away from the model of...
cues.zh: 在这个特定配置下，L2 缓存。在那之上，每个核心各自有独立的 L1 缓存。哦，重要的是，还有一个存储缓冲区，因为写总是比读开销更大，所以你真的很想缓存并缓冲这些写。而且，如果你眯着眼看对了，你会看到一片内存的山脉，每个山峰上都坐着一个核心。这离……的模型非常遥远

cues.en: Everybody talks directly to the memory and does it one at a time. There's a lot of indirection. And a lot of memory requests can be in flight at a time. For even this complexity to be manageable, we're going to make a key assumption, which I'm going to come back to later in the talk. We're going to make the assumption that all of these caches are coherent. There have been people who are experts who...
cues.zh: 大家都直接和内存通信，并且一次只进行一次。这中间有很多层间接访问。而且同时可能有很多内存请求在处理中。为了让这种复杂度也在可控范围内，我们要先做一个关键假设，我稍后在演讲中还会提到这一点。我们要假设所有这些缓存都是一致的。曾有一些专家……

cues.en: who have expressed the opinion that that is an assumption that is bound to fail because coherent caches don't scale. Therefore, as you get larger numbers of cores on die, that we're going to have to go away from coherent caches. This appears not to be true. And I'll point to a current reference at the end. But we're making this key assumption. Everything that I'm going to talk about in the complexity, it is merely that hard as long as we have coherent caches. And that safety net should continue.
cues.zh: ……他们表达过这样的观点：这个假设注定会破灭，因为一致性缓存无法扩展。因此，随着单芯片上核心数量的增加，我们必须放弃一致性缓存。事实证明这似乎并不属实。在最后我会给出一篇当下的参考资料。但我们先做这个关键假设。我接下来要讲的所有复杂性，只要我们有一致性缓存，难度也就仅仅如此而已。而且这个安全网应该会一直存在。

cues.en: So here's the talk in one slide. You can ignore pretty much the entire rest of this talk if you simply don't write a race condition and don't use non-default relaxed atomics. In that case, your code will do what you probably think it does. So why are we having this talk? Three reasons. First, sometimes compiler and hardware can have bugs. And when those bugs manifest, we may need to understand why and what they're doing. Second,
cues.zh: 这就是一张幻灯片讲完的内容。只要你完全不写出竞态条件，并且不使用非默认的宽松原子操作（relaxed atomics），基本上就可以忽略接下来整场演讲了。在这种情况下，代码的执行逻辑很可能就如你所想。那我们为什么还要做这场演讲呢？三个原因。首先，有时编译器和硬件会出现 bug。当这些 bug 暴露出来时，我们可能需要理解其原因和它们在干什么。其次，

cues.en: If there's a button, you want to push it. I know you do. You're advanced C++ developers. We can't help ourselves sometimes. So because there are relaxed atomics in the standard, we ask the question, what happens if I use this in combination with this? And so we're going to cover that. And sometimes you just want to have that level of control. So we're going to see why you sometimes may want to reach for those tools. So true or false, does your computer execute
cues.zh: 要是面前有个按钮，你就会想按下去。我知道你们会按的。你们都是资深的 C++ 开发者。我们有时就是忍不住。既然标准库里有宽松原子操作，我们就会问：如果我把它和这个混着用会怎样？所以我们也会探讨这个问题。另外，有时你只是想拥有那种控制力。所以我们来看看为什么有时你会想用这些工具。那么，判断对错：计算机是否在执行……

cues.en: the program you wrote in your source code, there is a hit on the screen. No, it doesn't. Why not? Well, if you think about what we call a sequentially consistent execution of your source code, that you can take your source code and read it as text, and know that the computer is actually going to do that, if it's multiple threads, that each thread will run in source code order exactly, and the result will be some interleaving, that's a very quaint concept. On Big Iron, we left that behind roughly in the 60s,
cues.zh: ……你在源代码中写的那个程序？屏幕上已经有提示了。不，它并没有。为什么呢？嗯，如果你考虑的是我们所谓的源代码顺序一致性执行——即你可以像读文本一样看源码，并确信计算机真的会照做；如果是多线程，每个线程都会严格按源码顺序执行，结果只是某种交替交织——这是个非常老派的概念。在大型机上，我们大约在 60 年代就抛弃了这个概念，

cues.en: If we, on PCs, we left that behind roughly after the 80s. Because we do all sorts of optimizations and transformations. Your code, what you wrote, and especially the memory accesses, the loads and stores you wrote, don't execute in the order that you said. That would be way too slow. You didn't mean to do that. So the compiler...
cues.zh: 而在 PC 上，我们大概在 80 年代后也告别了它。因为我们会做各种各样的优化和转换。你写的代码，尤其是你写下的内存访问、读取和写入操作，并没有按照你指定的顺序去执行。那样做实在太慢了。你也并不是真想那样。所以编译器……

cues.en: Or, so don't just blame the compiler, it could be the processor hardware, or don't just blame them, it could be the cache system and the cache effect. Say, no, no, no, you didn't really want to execute that program you wrote. No, you want to write, you want to execute a better program. Here, let me change it into that for you. The two key concepts we have to keep in mind. The first is this idea that I mentioned a minute ago, sequential consistency. So this was defined by Leslie Lamport back in 1979 as
cues.zh: 所以别只怪编译器，也可能是处理器硬件；也别只怪它们，还可能是缓存系统和缓存效应。就像说：不不不，你其实不想执行你写的那程序。不，你想写、想执行一个更好的程序。来，我帮你改成那个。我们必须记住两个关键概念。第一个是我刚才提到的顺序一致性。这是 Leslie Lamport 在 1979 年定义的：

cues.en: You execute your program, especially your loads and stores, your reads and writes to memory, in the order in which they would happen in a reading of the source code by the language rules. That's one definition. That would be ideal because the program would actually do what we expect. The second key concept, which is separate, a race condition, we covered this a bit yesterday, is when you have the same memory location or object and there's two threads that are not synchronized that can access it and at least one is a writer.
cues.zh: 你执行程序，尤其是加载和存储、对内存的读写，要按语言规则阅读源代码时它们会发生的顺序进行。这是一种定义。那会很理想，因为程序实际会做我们期望的事。第二个关键概念是另一个问题——竞态条件，我们昨天稍微讲过：同一个内存位置或对象，有两个未同步的线程都能访问它，并且至少有一个是写者。

cues.en: If they're both readers, you can read the bits all day and cache them. That's fine. But if at least one is a writer, then you can get torn writes. You can get out of order writes. You can see weird pink elephants. And we'll talk a bit more about pink elephants in a moment. So sequential consistency seems great. I mean, who wouldn't want the computer to execute the program you actually wrote? Debugging is hard enough, even with the program you wrote, right? So because it can be much more expensive to do what you wrote, we may want to reorder this.
cues.zh: 如果两个都是读者，你可以整天读这些位并缓存它们，没问题。但只要至少一个是写者，就可能出现撕裂写，可能出现乱序写，还可能看到奇怪的粉红大象。稍后我们会再谈一点粉红大象。所以顺序一致性看起来很棒。我是说，谁不希望计算机执行你真正写下的程序呢？就算程序是你写的，调试也已经够难了，对吧？但按你写的顺序做可能代价高得多，所以我们可能想重排。

cues.en: And they may have even other tricks up their sleeve that you can't know about that on particular hardware architectures may do the job much better. And the common reaction to that is, excuse me, what do you mean you'll think about executing the program I wrote or maybe run a different program for me. We'll come back to that at the end. One key thing to remember is that the only thing you care about is what you wrote in your source code and what actually happens. There's lots of space in between so that
cues.zh: 它们可能还有你根本不知道的招数，在特定硬件架构上能把活干得好得多。常见的反应是：不好意思，你说“考虑执行我写的程序”是什么意思？或者也许给我跑另一个程序？我们最后会回到这个问题。要记住的一个关键点是，你唯一关心的是源代码里写了什么，以及实际发生了什么。中间有很大的空间，所以

cues.en: the compiler may do things like common sub-expression elimination, register allocation. The processor may do pre-fetching, may do speculation, may overlap writes. The cache system may have store buffers, private shared caches. All sorts of things can happen, all of which have the effect of apparently reordering the memory reads and writes that your program said it was going to do. And you can't tell who did it, usually unless you dig real deep, but you don't care. All you care about is what you wrote,
cues.zh: 编译器可能做公共子表达式消除、寄存器分配之类的事。处理器可能做预取、推测执行、重叠写。缓存系统可能有存储缓冲区、私有共享缓存。各种事情都可能发生，效果上都会让你程序声称要做的内存读写看起来被重排了。通常你没法判断是谁干的，除非你挖得非常深，但你并不关心。你只关心你写了什么，

cues.en: and what actually gets executed, and as long as this is a valid execution of that, you're good, and you don't care who rearranged it from some other valid execution that might have happened. So all we want is that the actual execution be equivalent to some sequentially consistent interleaved execution of your threads, including that every read and write appears as though
cues.zh: 以及实际执行的是什么；只要这是对它的一个合法执行，你就没问题，你也不关心是谁把它从可能发生的另一个合法执行重排成了这样。所以我们想要的是：实际执行等价于你的线程某种顺序一致的交错执行，包括每一次读写看起来都像是

cues.en: You did it atomically and globally so that one processor is using the main memory at a time. The goal is to try to maintain this illusion because none of us want to be disillusioned. So a key thing to remember is that transformations at each of those levels are equivalent, which is really important because it turns out that means that it doesn't matter if it's the cache effect that's doing it. It doesn't matter if the processor is doing it or the compiler.
cues.zh: 你原子且全局地完成了它，从而同一时间只有一个处理器在使用主存。目标就是尽量维持这个幻觉，因为没人想被幻灭。所以要记住的关键点是：每个层级的变换都是等价的；这非常重要，因为事实证明，这意味着不管是缓存效应在这么做，还是处理器在这么做，或者编译器在这么做，都无所谓。

cues.en: You can reason about all of these transformations by looking at sample source code and saying, what if these lines were moved around? And in fact, memory model designers do this all the time. And they talk about memory models in terms of their effects and transformations on source code, which is good because it's something we can actually understand. So that's what we're going to follow, starting with this example. How many of you have seen Decker's algorithm or its variants like Peterson's algorithm before? Quite a few. OK.
cues.zh: 大家可以通过查看示例源码来推导所有这些变换，心想：如果这几行代码换个顺序会怎样？事实上，内存模型设计者们一直都在这么做。他们通过对源码产生的效果和变换来讨论内存模型，这很好，因为这是我们真正能理解的东西。所以我们接下来就采用这种方式，先来看这个例子。有多少人以前见过 Decker 算法，或者像 Peterson 算法这样的变体？不少人啊，好的。

cues.en: The idea here is this is in the land before locks, the land before mutexes, where we had to do synchronization ourselves. The idea here is we have two flags that let two threads stay off each other's toes getting into a critical region. You don't want both threads in the critical region at the same time because that would be erased. Maybe one's reading, one's writing, they're both writing. So what they do is they do the following little dance.
cues.zh: 这里的核心思想是，在那个还没有锁、没有互斥量的年代，我们必须自己来实现同步。这里的思路是用两个标志位，让两个线程在进入临界区时不会踩到对方的脚。你肯定不希望两个线程同时进入临界区，因为那样会引发竞态。可能一个在读一个在写，或者都在写。所以它们遵循的是下面这样一套交戈步骤。

cues.en: Thread 1 says, I'm going to set my flag to true. What this does is it declares my intent to enter the critical section. I haven't done it yet. I'm just declaring, hey, Buster, I want to get in. Then I look at the other thread's flag to see if he has already declared his intent to enter. If he has, I'll have to back off and try again later, do some sort of back off. But if he hasn't,
cues.zh: 线程 1 说，我要把我的标志位设为 true。这样做的目的是声明我想进入临界区的意图。我还没真正进去呢。我只是声明一下：“嘿，伙计，我想进去了。” 然后我去查看另一个线程的标志位，看他是否也已经声明了进入的意图。如果他声明了，那我就得退让一步稍后再试，做某种退避操作。但如果他还没声明，

cues.en: Then it's safe for me to go into the critical section. Why? Because he's doing the same dance. Before he goes into his critical section, he's going to set his flag to declare his intent to enter. I know that flag wasn't set before, so I'm going in. Then he sets it. I know he'll see. Then when he looks over, he'll see my flag is already set, and he'll back off. So I set my flag. Then I look at his. If he hasn't set it, then it's safe for me to go in, and vice versa for thread two.
